summary.summary: Herefordshire's 2025/26 treasury outturn (Appendix C to Cabinet on 21 May 2026) shows a council running heavily on internal borrowing: its Capital Financing Requirement of £330.8m at 31 March 2026 sits well above external long-term borrowing of £185.1m, though it drew a new £55.0m 10-year loan at 4.83% in the final quarter and flagged more borrowing to come, driven by the capital programme and the ongoing cost of financing its DSG schools deficit (not quantified in this report). Treasury investments stood at £57.1m at a 4.60% average, and investment income of £2.534m beat a £0.552m budget by £1.982m, helped by high-rate short deposits with other local authorities (up to 7.00%). All prudential and treasury indicators were complied with: external debt of £231.2m sat well within the £420m authorised limit, financing costs held at 10% of net revenue, and only 7% of borrowing matures within 12 months. The council also earns about £1.8m a year in loan interest from its waste-disposal PFI provider.

signals.headline: New £55.0m 10-year loan drawn at 4.83% in the final quarter of 2025/26 lifts long-term borrowing to £185.1m at 31 March 2026, with further borrowing flagged for the capital programme and DSG-deficit financing
signals.why: After years of internal borrowing the council is now taking material external long-term debt at above-5% market levels, with more signalled.

signals.headline: The council states its final-quarter 2025/26 borrowing was driven partly by 'the ongoing impact of financing the DSG deficit' (para 4.2); the deficit itself is not quantified in this treasury appendix
signals.why: The schools deficit is converting into real external borrowing need, though its size must be read from the revenue/accounts monitoring rather than this report.

compliance.notes: Strong, comprehensive 2026/27 strategy for a mid-size unitary borrower: full prudential-indicator set with an exemplary 70-year liability benchmark, a robust creditworthiness/investment framework, clear MRP policy and full CIPFA Code adoption. Weakest areas are the commercial/non-treasury disclosure suite (thin, reflecting the council's small ~1% commercial exposure) and a few specific omissions - no distinct fixed/variable interest-rate exposure limits, no quantitative investment risk indicator, no sterling-only or third-party/pension-monies statements.

Capital Strategy p.12-14 paras 7.8/8 (scheme selection, due diligence, project-board monitoring) function as de facto investment practices

news_drafts.headline: Herefordshire's SEND plan approved, with £32.7m high needs grant due on 30 November
news_drafts.lead:
Herefordshire Council was told on 2 October 2026 that its plan for reforming support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) has been approved. It is due £32.7m of High Needs Stability Grant on 30 November. The grant covers 90% of the deficits built up on the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, up to 31 March 2026. The council submitted the plan on 19 June, in line with the deadline, and payment had been expected in autumn, subject to approval.

The council will meet the other 10%, about £3.6m, from money set aside for named purposes (earmarked reserves). The DSG deficit stood at £36.3m at the end of 2025/26, below the £38.2m forecast for March 2026. At quarter 1, the council forecast a 2026/27 overspend of £25.7m, all in high needs, the part of school funding for SEND. The schools, central and early years blocks are forecast at budget. At budget setting the council had expected an in-year deficit of £25.9m. The papers attribute the £0.2m difference to fewer complex needs placements, partly offset by higher top-up payments for pupils in mainstream schools. The forecast cumulative deficit at March 2027 is £62.0m in the Schools Forum report and £62.2m in the deficit management plan. The forecasts exclude the grant.

The cumulative deficit is held as an unusable reserve, under a statutory instrument that remains in place until 31 March 2028. A revised three-year DSG Deficit Management Plan has been approved. It does not assume the deficit can be eliminated within three years and aims to slow its growth.
news_drafts.paper_title: Schools Forum Report - DSG 2026-27 Quarter 1 Update

news_drafts.headline: Herefordshire's schools funding deficit reached £36.3m in March 2026, up from £20.0m a year earlier
news_drafts.lead:
Herefordshire Council's deficit on the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) stood at £36.3m on 31 March 2026, up from £20.0m a year before. The Audit and Governance Committee, which met on 29 September, had the figure in its external auditor's annual report and the council's own governance statement. The auditor puts it at about 45% of the council's usable reserves (the part of its reserves it can actually spend) and notes it is well above the council's £10.1m general fund balance.

The council's governance statement attributes £16.3m of the rise to an overspend in the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The council forecasts further in-year deficits of £26.0m in 2026/27 and £24.7m in 2027/28. The auditor says this is a continuing weakness from the previous year, and that it was raised as a key recommendation in 2024-25 and has been raised again.

In June 2026 the council submitted a SEND Reform Plan to the Department for Education, seeking a High Needs Stability Grant. If approved, the grant would cover about 90% of the accumulated deficit, or £32.7m. The remaining £3.6m would fall to the council when the statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps such deficits off a council's main balance sheet, ends in March 2028. The auditor notes continuing uncertainty over how national reform of SEND funding will affect the council's future position.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix A Herefordshire Auditors Annual Report 2025-26

news_drafts.headline: Herefordshire expects government grant to cover 90% (£32.7m) of schools deficit, leaving £3.6m from 2028
news_drafts.lead:
Herefordshire Council expects a new government grant to cover about £32.7m, or 90%, of its schools-funding deficit, leaving the council liable for the remaining £3.6m from March 2028. Cabinet's quarter-one budget report, considered on 24 September, says the Department for Education (DfE) would pay the High Needs Stability Grant, subject to its approval. The grant is expected in autumn 2026.

The deficit is on the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools; it is mostly an overspend on support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). It stood at £36.3m at the start of the year. With a deficit budget of £25.9m approved for 2026/27, the report says the total will reach £62.2m by 31 March 2027 if spending is contained. The council sent its Local SEND Reform Plan to the DfE on 19 June 2026. The £3.6m falls to the council when the statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps such deficits off a council's main balance sheet, ends in March 2028.

The council is also spending £10m on buildings in 2026/27: £5m to relocate the Pupil Referral Unit and £5m for a new Alternative Provision Centre. It has confirmed a £3.8m top-up to high needs capital funding over three years, which the risk register says "falls short of what is required to meet demand".

findings.paper_title: DSG Deficit Management Plan and SEND Reforms
findings.headline: Westfield rebuild or expansion to add 45 places, phased over four years.
findings.detail: The sufficiency table lists this as all-age SLD, PMLD and complex specialist capacity. The risk register names capital delivery slippage as a risk that would delay place creation and extend reliance on independent and out-of-area placements.
findings.matters: The timing of place creation sets when placement savings can start, so a delay in capital delivery moves the whole recovery timetable.
findings.figures: 45 additional places over four years; Ryefield MLD 55 places by 2030; SEMH special school 80 places by 2030
findings.quote: 45 additional places phased over four years.

findings.paper_title: DSG Deficit Management Plan and SEND Reforms
findings.headline: Transport is not counted as a saving unless it is evidenced through transport reporting.
findings.detail: The paper treats transport as a separate impact area tracked through Home to School Transport governance. Travel impact assessments are to be applied to all new SEND and AP proposals.
findings.matters: Transport can offset placement savings, so how a council treats it changes the net saving that a peer or lender would compare.
findings.quote: Transport is included as a separate impact area and will not be assumed as a saving unless evidenced through

findings.paper_title: DSG Deficit Management Plan and SEND Reforms
findings.headline: AP pupils rose from 134 in 2024 to 254 in 2025 and 360 in 2026, against 64 statutory AP places.
findings.detail: The paper gives current AP demand as around 100 pupils against 64 statutory places. AP placements are shown rising from 137 to 274 and then 430 over the same period, and the sufficiency plan relies on HPRS relocation and expansion.
findings.matters: AP is both a pressure and the planned solution here, and growth in pupil numbers ahead of places is a cost driver other councils will recognise.
findings.figures: AP pupils 134 (2024), 254 (2025), 360 (2026); AP placements 137, 274, 430; 64 statutory AP places; demand around 100 pupils
findings.quote: AP pupils rose from 134 in 2024 to 254 in 2025 and 360 in 2026

findings.paper_title: DSG Deficit Management Plan and SEND Reforms
findings.headline: EHCP baseline of 2,048 forecast to rise to 3,842 by 2029, an increase of 1,424.
findings.detail: The paper uses SEN2 2026 as the baseline. Its KPI for EHCP numbers is no more than +10% by Year 3, which sits against the 2029 forecast of 3,842 in the same document.
findings.matters: Demand growth of this scale drives the High Needs cost base, and the gap between the forecast and the stated numeric target is what a peer would want explained.
findings.figures: 2,048 EHCPs baseline; 3,842 forecast by 2029; increase of 1,424; 70% increase; KPI no more than +10% by Year 3
findings.quote: reform data template uses 2,048 EHCPs as the baseline (SEN2 2026) and forecasts 3,842 EHCPs by 2029, an increase of 1,424 by 2029.

findings.paper_title: DSG Deficit Management Plan and SEND Reforms
findings.headline: Plan budgets 110 growth placements in independent provision in 2026/27, with a Year 3 target to reduce the share of EHCP pupils in independent placements from 12.1% to 8%.
findings.detail: The paper says 231 independent or non-maintained placements are budgeted for 2026/27, including 110 growth placements. The KPI table sets a baseline of 12.1% and a Year 3 target of 8%.
findings.matters: A finance director would test whether budgeted growth in 2026/27 is reconciled with the Year 3 reduction target in later monitoring, given the cost difference per placement.
findings.figures: 231 placements budgeted; 110 growth placements in 2026/27; 12.1% baseline; 8% Year 3 target; £56,000 core comparator
findings.quote: 231 placements budgeted with 110 growth placements throughout 2026/27
